Due to rapidly deteriorating meteorological conditions at the destination, the flight crew initiated a diversion to the alternate airport at 13:58:12 EST.

1.3 The flight was conducted in accordance with the operational requirements of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121. The flight plan was filed under instrument flight rules (IFR) and included standard alternate airport selection criteria per 14 CFR 121.619. Air traffic control (ATC) communications were recorded on the Boston Center and approach control frequencies. The final ATC transmission from the flight crew occurred at 14:19:05 EST, during which the crew reported severe airframe icing and requested priority handling for the approach. Radar data indicated the aircraft was established on a 3.0° glide slope at 1,800 feet MSL, with a ground speed of 142 knots, prior to the loss of radar contact at 14:21:48 EST.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 The Captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 2847193, with multi-engine land and instrument airplane ratings. The Captain possessed a type rating for the DHC-8-400 and had accumulated 8,450 total flight hours, of which 2,120 hours were in the accident aircraft type. The Captain’s most recent line check was completed on January 15, 2023, with a satisfactory evaluation. The Captain’s most recent proficiency check, conducted in a Level D full-flight simulator, was completed on February 10, 2023. The simulator session included training on severe icing recognition, asymmetric ice shedding, and recovery from high-angle-of-attack conditions. The Captain’s medical certificate was first-class, issued on November 22, 2022, with no limitations.

2.2 The First Officer held an ATP certificate, certificate number 3192847, with multi-engine land and instrument airplane ratings, and possessed a DHC-8-400 type rating. The First Officer had accumulated 3,210 total flight hours, with 1,450 hours in type. The First Officer’s most recent line-oriented flight training (LOFT) session was completed on December 20, 2022, and included scenario-based training for winter operations and diversion decision-making. Both crewmembers were current and qualified in accordance with 14 CFR 121.433 and 121.437. The First Officer’s medical certificate was first-class, issued on October 5, 2022, with no limitations.

2.3 Review of the crewmembers’ duty and rest records indicated compliance with 14 CFR Part 117 flight and duty limitations. The Captain had been on duty for 6 hours and 15 minutes at the time of the accident, with a scheduled rest period of 10 hours prior to the duty day. The First Officer had been on duty for 5 hours and 40 minutes, with a scheduled rest period of 11 hours prior to the duty day. Both crewmembers reported adequate rest and no use of prescription or over-the-counter medications that would impair performance. Training records indicated that both pilots had completed the operator’s annual winter operations ground school module on January 8, 2023, which covered supercooled large droplet (SLD) icing, de-icing boot limitations, and emergency diversion protocols.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 The accident aircraft was a De Havilland Canada DHC-8-400, manufacturer serial number 4567, manufactured in 2018. At the time of the accident, the aircraft had accumulated 18,452 total airframe hours and 14,210 total flight cycles. The aircraft was equipped with two Rolls-Royce AE 2100D3 turboprop engines, each rated at 5,071 shaft horsepower. The propellers were Hamilton Sundstrand 14SF-19, six-blade, constant-speed, full-feathering units. The aircraft’s maximum takeoff weight was 64,500 pounds, and the operating weight at the time of the accident was calculated at 58,210 pounds.

3.2 The aircraft’s maintenance records were reviewed and found to be current. The most recent heavy maintenance check (C-check) was completed on November 12, 2022, at 17,890 airframe hours. All applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) were documented as complied with, including AD 2021-14-08 (Ice Protection System Inspection) and AD 2022-09-12 (Propeller Anti-Ice Element Replacement). The ice protection system (IPS) was inspected during the C-check and found to be within manufacturer tolerances. The pneumatic de-icing boots, propeller anti-ice system, and engine inlet anti-ice system were operational at the time of the last scheduled maintenance. No deferred maintenance items related to the IPS or flight control systems were recorded in the aircraft logbook.

3.3 The aircraft’s ice protection system was designed to operate in accordance with the aircraft flight manual (AFM) limitations. The system utilized engine bleed air routed to the wing and empennage de-icing boots, with a cyclic inflation sequence of 6 seconds on, 6 seconds off. The propeller and engine inlet anti-ice systems utilized electrical heating elements and bleed air, respectively. Maintenance logs indicated that the operator’s engineering department, in coordination with Rolls-Royce, had previously issued a fleet-wide service information letter (SIL-2022-04) regarding ice accretion monitoring procedures for the AE 2100D3 engine series. The SIL recommended increased inspection intervals for engine inlet guide vanes when operating in known SLD conditions.

3.4 The operator’s maintenance and training infrastructure also supports a mixed fleet, including the Boeing 737 MAX 9. While the Boeing 737 MAX 9 utilizes a different ice protection architecture (primarily thermal anti-ice for engine inlets and wing leading edges), the operator’s centralized training division cross-referenced icing event data across both turboprop and jet platforms to standardize crew recognition protocols. Maintenance tooling and calibration equipment for the DHC-8-400 were stored at the same facility as the Boeing 737 MAX 9 fleet, with separate inventory tracking and quality assurance procedures. No maintenance discrepancies were noted for the accident aircraft’s flight control or ice protection systems in the 30 days preceding the accident.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 At the time of the accident, a low-pressure system was tracking across the northeastern United States, producing widespread stratiform precipitation and freezing rain. Surface observations at the alternate airport, recorded at 14:00 EST, indicated a temperature of -2°C, a dew point of -3°C, visibility of 1.5 statute miles in light freezing rain, and an overcast ceiling at 1,200 feet above ground level (AGL). The wind was from 240° at 12 knots, gusting to 18 knots. The altimeter setting was 29.84 inches of mercury (inHg).

4.2 The Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) for the alternate airport, issued at 11:00 EST, forecasted conditions of 2,000 feet broken, 4,000 feet overcast, with light freezing rain and temperatures between -1°C and -4°C through 18:00 EST. En route weather radar data indicated a continuous band of moderate to heavy precipitation extending from the departure airport to the alternate, with reflectivity values between 35 and 45 dBZ. The freezing level was at 2,800 feet MSL, with a temperature inversion between 3,000 and 5,000 feet MSL.

4.3 Pilot reports (PIREPs) filed by preceding traffic between 13:15 and 13:50 EST documented moderate to severe rime and clear ice accumulation on airframe surfaces at altitudes between 4,000 and 8,000 feet MSL. At 13:58:12 EST, the accident flight crew transmitted a PIREP reporting severe airframe icing, with ice accumulation exceeding 1 inch on unprotected surfaces, and requested an immediate diversion to the alternate airport. The flight crew reported a degradation in climb performance, increased control forces, and a 15-knot reduction in indicated airspeed for a given power setting.

4.4 Atmospheric sounding data from the nearest upper-air observation station indicated a layer of supercooled large droplets (SLD) present between 4,500 and 6,500 feet MSL. The liquid water content (LWC) was estimated at 0.8 to 1.2 grams per cubic meter, with median volume diameters (MVD) exceeding 50 microns. The presence of SLD conditions is known to produce ice accretion aft of standard de-icing boot coverage areas, resulting in aerodynamic degradation and increased stall speeds. The National Weather Service issued an AIRMET Zulu for moderate icing between 3,000 and 9,000 feet MSL, valid from 12:00 to 18:00 EST.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 The aircraft impacted a heavily wooded, rolling terrain feature at an elevation of 1,420 feet MSL. The initial impact point was characterized by a 12-foot-long, 4-foot-wide ground scar oriented on a magnetic heading of 235°. The primary wreckage distribution extended approximately 320 feet along a debris path aligned with the initial impact heading. The fuselage came to rest inverted, with the nose section fragmented and the empennage separated from the aft fuselage. The main landing gear was found retracted, with the left main gear assembly displaced 18 feet aft of the initial impact point.

5.2 Examination of the impact site revealed multiple tree strikes consistent with a high-angle, high-velocity descent. The first tree strike occurred 45 feet prior to the initial ground impact, with a 14-inch diameter pine tree severed at a height of 28 feet. The angle of the tree strike indicated a descent path of approximately 18° below the horizon. Control surface positions were documented at the scene: the left aileron was found in a neutral position, the right aileron was deflected 12° upward, and both elevators were found in a trailing-edge-down position. The rudder was found deflected 8° to the left. The flap selector was found in the 15° position, with the left wing flaps extended to 12° and the right wing flaps extended to 14°.

5.3 Post-impact examination of recovered airframe components revealed significant ice accretion on the leading edges of the wings, horizontal stabilizer, and vertical fin. The de-icing boots on the left wing were found in a partially inflated state, with ice bridging observed between adjacent boot segments. The right wing boots were found fully deflated. Ice thickness measurements on the wing leading edge, aft of the boot coverage, ranged from 0.75 to 1.25 inches. The propeller blades exhibited leading-edge erosion and ice shedding damage consistent with asymmetric ice accumulation. The engine inlet guide vanes showed no evidence of foreign object damage, but ice residue was present on the inner surfaces.

5.4 The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were recovered and transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for readout. Preliminary FDR data indicated that at 14:18:32 EST, the aircraft was established on a 3.0° glide slope at 1,800 feet MSL, with an indicated airspeed of 135 knots. At 14:19:45 EST, the indicated airspeed decreased to 118 knots, and the pitch attitude increased to 14° nose-up. At 14:20:12 EST, the stick shaker activated, followed by a rapid increase in angle of attack to 18.5°. The aircraft subsequently entered an uncommanded left roll, with bank angle exceeding 45° within 4 seconds. Engine torque parameters remained within normal operating limits until impact. The CVR captured the flight crew’s discussion of ice accumulation, activation of the anti-ice system, and execution of the diversion checklist.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 The operator’s standard operating procedures (SOPs) for flight in icing conditions, as outlined in the company operations manual, required immediate activation of the ice protection system upon entry into visible moisture with temperatures at or below +5°C. The SOPs mandated a minimum airspeed increase of 10 knots above the normal approach speed when operating in known or forecast icing conditions. The manual also specified that if severe icing is encountered, the flight crew should exit the icing conditions immediately by changing altitude or heading, and declare an emergency if necessary. The operator’s dispatch release included a specific icing advisory for the route, with recommended minimum altitudes and alternate airport weather minima.

6.2 The operator’s training program included simulator-based scenarios for severe icing encounters, emphasizing the recognition of ice accretion on unprotected surfaces, the potential for aerodynamic degradation, and the execution of recovery procedures. The training curriculum was developed in accordance with Advisory Circular (AC) 120-58, Large Aircraft Ground Deicing, and AC 120-60, In-Flight Icing. The operator’s safety management system (SMS) had previously tracked three icing-related events within the preceding 24 months, all of which resulted in successful diversions without incident. The SMS database indicated that 87% of reported icing events occurred during the descent phase, with 62% involving SLD conditions.

6.3 The aircraft was originally certified under 14 CFR Part 25, with specific compliance demonstrated for flight in icing conditions. The certification basis included compliance with 14 CFR 25.571, Damage-Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure, which requires that the aircraft structure be evaluated for residual strength and crack growth under repeated loading conditions, including those induced by ice accretion and asymmetric shedding. The operator’s continuing airworthiness program incorporated fatigue monitoring and structural inspections aligned with the requirements of 14 CFR 25.571. The aircraft’s structural repair manual (SRM) provided specific guidance for post-icing inspection of wing spars and control surface hinges.

6.4 The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued multiple airworthiness directives and safety alerts regarding in-flight icing, particularly concerning supercooled large droplet (SLD) conditions. The NTSB has previously investigated accidents involving regional turboprop aircraft where ice accumulation aft of de-icing boots resulted in aerodynamic stall at speeds above the published stall speed. The investigation into this accident will include a detailed analysis of the ice protection system performance, crew decision-making, and meteorological data to determine the sequence of events leading to the loss of control. All factual data collected will be compiled and analyzed in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, with findings documented in subsequent factual reports and safety recommendations as warranted.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the NTSB Flight Data Recorder, Materials, and Structures Groups in support of the investigation into the March 3, 2023, loss of control and terrain impact involving a regional turboprop aircraft. The scope of this examination encompasses the recovery, readout, and parameter validation of the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR), metallurgical and elastomeric evaluation of the pneumatic de-icing boot assemblies, structural integrity assessment of the left wing leading edge slat track, and correlation of recorded flight parameters with manufacturer performance envelopes.

The examination was conducted between March 15 and March 24, 2023, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and the FDR/CVR Readout Facility in Ashburn, Virginia. Items examined included:
- Solid-state FDR, Part Number (P/N) 2100-4000-00, Serial Number (S/N) 88421
- Cockpit voice recorder, P/N 93A1000-01, S/N 77219
- Left wing outboard pneumatic de-icing boot, P/N 45-8821-03, S/N 11944
- Right wing inboard pneumatic de-icing boot, P/N 45-8821-03, S/N 11945
- Wing leading edge slat track assembly, P/N 72-440-11, S/N 0882
- Engine torque transducer, P/N 331-004-00, S/N 55102

All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB Standard Operating Procedures, RTCA DO-178C/DO-254 software/hardware validation guidelines, and ASTM/SAE material testing standards. The investigation team coordinated with the aircraft manufacturer, engine OEM, and component suppliers to verify baseline specifications and operational limits. Comparative industry data, including maintenance tracking protocols utilized by Southwest Airlines and operational icing encounter databases maintained by Ethiopian Airlines, were referenced to contextualize component wear rates and environmental exposure histories.

2. BACKGROUND

The accident aircraft is a twin-engine, high-wing regional turboprop configured for 68 passengers, certified under 14 CFR Part 25. The airframe incorporates a conventional pneumatic de-icing system (PDS) utilizing inflatable elastomeric boots bonded to the leading edges of the wings, horizontal stabilizer, and vertical fin. The PDS operates via engine-driven pneumatic pumps, pressure-regulating valves, and a sequenced timer module that cycles individual boot segments to fracture and shed accreted ice. System design and certification compliance were established per FAA Advisory Circular 25.1419-2D and SAE ARP 5905, with structural fatigue and damage tolerance evaluations conducted in accordance with Section 25.571.

The FDR and voice recorder are integrated into a unified crash-protected memory architecture, recording 256 discrete parameters at 1 Hz and 4 Hz sampling rates, respectively. The CVR captures four discrete audio channels (captain, first officer, observer, and area microphone) with a continuous 2-hour loop. Both units are housed in titanium alloy enclosures rated for 3,400 G impact, 1,100°C fire exposure for 60 minutes, and 20,000 ft MSL hydrostatic pressure.

The accident aircraft, S/N 4482, accumulated 18,450 flight hours and 22,100 flight cycles at the time of the event. The most recent heavy maintenance inspection (C-check) was completed on January 12, 2023, during which the pneumatic de-icing boots were replaced per Service Bulletin 72-0045. The FDR and CVR were last calibrated on November 8, 2022, with all parameter drift values within ±0.5% of manufacturer specifications. Operational records indicate the aircraft was routinely deployed in high-latitude and high-altitude environments, with documented exposure to supercooled large droplet (SLD) conditions on 142 occasions over the preceding 24 months.

Structural certification of the wing leading edge assembly adhered to Section 25.571 damage tolerance requirements, incorporating crack propagation modeling, residual strength analysis, and fail-safe load path verification. The slat track assembly utilizes 7075-T6 aluminum alloy with anodized surface treatment and is fastened with titanium Hi-Lok collars torqued to 185 ± 10 in-lbs. The pneumatic boots are fabricated from a polyurethane-based elastomer compound (DuPont Hypalon 40S equivalent) with a nominal thickness of 0.185 inches, designed to withstand cyclic inflation pressures of 18 ± 2 PSI and temperature excursions from -55°C to +70°C.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

The FDR and voice recorder were recovered from the impact site with moderate external casing deformation. The memory modules were extracted, cleaned per RTCA DO-160G environmental conditioning protocols, and interfaced with the manufacturer's proprietary readout system. No data corruption or memory cell degradation was identified. The CVR audio channels were demodulated, time-aligned with FDR parameters, and subjected to spectral analysis to isolate system warnings, switch actuations, and crew communications.

Physical examination of the left wing outboard pneumatic de-icing boot (P/N 45-8821-03, S/N 11944) revealed extensive surface erosion, micro-fissuring, and localized delamination along the chordwise inflation channels. Thickness measurements, taken at 12 discrete stations using a calibrated ultrasonic gauge (P/N UT-3000, ±0.001 in accuracy), indicated a mean thickness of 0.142 inches, representing a 23.2% reduction from the nominal 0.185-inch specification. The right wing inboard boot (S/N 11945) exhibited similar degradation, with a mean thickness of 0.148 inches.

Tensile testing was conducted per ASTM D412-16, utilizing Type C dumbbell specimens extracted from non-critical boot regions. The left wing specimen demonstrated an ultimate tensile strength of 2,850 PSI and an elongation at break of 185%, compared to the manufacturer's minimum specification of 3,200 PSI and 220% elongation. The right wing specimen yielded 2,910 PSI and 192% elongation. Hardness testing per ASTM D2240-15 (Shore A) recorded values of 68 and 70, respectively, against a baseline of 75 ± 3.

Chemical analysis via scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM/EDS) identified significant plasticizer migration and oxidative chain scission within the elastomer matrix. The presence of ozone-induced cracking was confirmed at depths of 0.003 to 0.005 inches, consistent with prolonged exposure to high-UV, low-temperature environments. Cross-sectional imaging (NTSB Photo Reference 2023-03-004 through 009) revealed interfacial debonding between the elastomer and the underlying adhesive primer layer, particularly along the inflation channel radii where cyclic stress concentrations are highest.

Pneumatic pressure decay testing was performed per SAE AS5711, utilizing a calibrated test rig with a 0.1% full-scale accuracy pressure transducer. The left wing boot was pressurized to 18 PSI and isolated. Pressure decayed to 12 PSI in 4.2 seconds, exceeding the manufacturer's allowable limit of a 3 PSI drop over 10 seconds. The right wing boot exhibited a decay to 13 PSI in 5.1 seconds. Valve response time testing indicated a 1.8-second delay in solenoid actuation, attributed to degraded O-ring compression set (measured at 28%, spec: ≤15%).

Structural examination of the left wing slat track assembly (P/N 72-440-11, S/N 0882) revealed no evidence of fatigue cracking, fastener failure, or plastic deformation. Non-destructive testing (NDT) via eddy current and fluorescent penetrant inspection (ASTM E1444/E165) confirmed compliance with Section 25.571 damage tolerance thresholds. The titanium Hi-Lok fasteners were extracted and torque-verified; all values fell within 178 to 192 in-lbs, consistent with installation specifications.

The engine torque transducer (P/N 331-004-00, S/N 55102) was bench-tested per RTCA DO-160G Section 16. Output linearity was verified across a 0 to 100% torque range, with a maximum deviation of 0.32% from the calibration curve. No internal short circuits, wire chafing, or connector pin corrosion were observed.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

FDR parameter extraction and time-synchronization with the voice recorder audio stream enabled precise reconstruction of the flight profile from 14:18:00 UTC to 14:28:15 UTC. The aircraft was operating at 11,500 ft MSL, descending on a 3.0° glidepath toward the alternate runway, with an indicated airspeed of 148 KIAS and a true airspeed of 162 KTAS. Outside air temperature (OAT) was recorded at -4°C, with total air temperature (TAT) at +1°C, indicating visible moisture and high probability of supercooled liquid water (SLW) accretion.

At 14:22:15 UTC, the ice detection system (IDS) triggered a continuous alert, and the flight crew manually engaged the pneumatic de-icing system. FDR data indicates the PDS sequencer initiated a 6-second inflation cycle across all wing segments. However, pressure transducer data reveals an asymmetric pressure distribution: the left wing outboard segment reached 16.2 PSI, while the right wing inboard segment peaked at 18.4 PSI. The pressure differential of 2.2 PSI persisted through three consecutive cycles, correlating with the degraded elastomer properties and delayed valve response identified during physical examination.

At 14:24:30 UTC, the aircraft entered a region of moderate to severe icing, as confirmed by CVR audio capturing the first officer's callout: "Heavy ice on the leading edge, boots not shedding." FDR parameters show a gradual increase in pitch attitude from 2.1° to 4.8° nose-up, accompanied by a 12-knot decay in indicated airspeed over 90 seconds. The autopilot remained engaged in vertical speed mode, commanding a -800 ft/min descent rate.

At 14:26:10 UTC, the roll trim position deviated 3.2° left, indicating asymmetric lift degradation. The flight control computer (FCC) recorded a roll moment of 1,180 ft-lbs, approaching the certified limit of 1,250 ft-lbs for the configuration. The crew disengaged the autopilot and manually applied right aileron and rudder input. FDR data shows control surface deflections of 14° right aileron and 8° right rudder, insufficient to counteract the rolling moment.

At 14:27:45 UTC, the stick shaker activated, coinciding with an airspeed of 118 KIAS and a pitch attitude of 7.2° nose-up. The angle of attack (AOA) vane data, sampled at 4 Hz, indicates a left wing AOA of 16.8° and a right wing AOA of 14.1°, confirming asymmetric stall onset. The CVR captures the captain's command: "Power, power, nose down," followed by a rapid increase in engine torque from 1,850 ft-lbs to 2,410 ft-lbs. Propeller RPM remained at 1,200, with beta angle transitioning to 12° reverse pitch at 14:28:02 UTC, indicating an attempted go-around maneuver.

At 14:28:12 UTC, the aircraft descended below 800 ft AGL, with a vertical speed of -2,400 ft/min and a bank angle of 28° left. The FDR recorded a final ground speed of 102 knots and a pitch attitude of 11.3° nose-up before data termination at 14:28:15 UTC. The voice recorder captured the final 1.2 seconds of impact acoustics, with no evidence of structural failure or system warnings prior to terrain contact.

Comparative analysis with normal operational parameters, derived from manufacturer flight test data and fleet performance databases maintained by Ethiopian Airlines, indicates that the observed airspeed decay and roll moment exceed standard icing encounter profiles by 34% and 28%, respectively. The delayed PDS response and asymmetric pressure distribution align with the elastomer degradation findings, reducing ice shedding efficiency by an estimated 40-50%. Structural load validation methodologies, analogous to those applied to the Boeing 737 MAX 9 wingbox fatigue monitoring systems, confirm that the airframe remained within certified load limits until aerodynamic stall onset.

5. SUMMARY

The examination and analysis of the flight data recorder, voice recorder, pneumatic de-icing components, and wing structural assemblies yielded the following factual findings:

- The FDR and CVR memory modules were recovered intact, with no data corruption or parameter drift exceeding manufacturer tolerances. Time-synchronized data reconstruction confirms a continuous flight profile from cruise descent through terrain impact.
- The pneumatic de-icing boots exhibited significant elastomer degradation, including a 23.2% reduction in mean thickness, tensile strength below specification (2,850 PSI vs. 3,200 PSI minimum), and Shore A hardness values of 68-70. SEM/EDS analysis confirmed oxidative chain scission, plasticizer migration, and ozone-induced micro-fissuring.
- Pneumatic pressure decay testing revealed a 6 PSI drop in 4.2 seconds on the left wing outboard segment, exceeding the allowable 3 PSI drop over 10 seconds. Solenoid valve response was delayed by 1.8 seconds due to O-ring compression set degradation.
- FDR data indicates asymmetric PDS pressure distribution (2.2 PSI differential) during icing encounter, correlating with delayed ice shedding and asymmetric lift degradation. Roll moment reached 1,180 ft-lbs, with left wing AOA exceeding 16.8° prior to stall warning activation.
- The aircraft's airspeed decayed from 148 KIAS to 118 KIAS over 5 minutes and 30 seconds, with pitch attitude increasing to 7.2° nose-up. Stick shaker activation occurred at 14:27:45 UTC, followed by manual control inputs and attempted go-around power application.
- Structural examination of the left wing slat track assembly revealed no fatigue cracking, fastener failure, or plastic deformation. NDT results confirm compliance with Section 25.571 damage tolerance requirements. All Hi-Lok fasteners were within torque specification (178-192 in-lbs).
- The engine torque transducer demonstrated linear output within 0.32% of calibration curve, with no evidence of electrical or mechanical failure.
- CVR audio analysis confirms crew awareness of severe icing conditions, manual PDS engagement, and standard stall recovery procedures. No system malfunctions or abnormal warnings were recorded prior to aerodynamic stall onset.
- Comparative operational data from Ethiopian Airlines and maintenance tracking protocols utilized by Southwest Airlines indicate that the observed elastomer degradation and pressure decay rates are consistent with prolonged exposure to high-UV, low-temperature environments and cyclic inflation stress.
- Structural load validation methodologies, consistent with those applied to the Boeing 737 MAX 9 airframe monitoring systems, confirm that the wing structure remained within certified load envelopes until aerodynamic stall conditions were reached.

All findings are presented as factual observations derived from physical examination, laboratory testing, and recorded data analysis. No determination of probable cause is included in this report.

INTERVIEW OF MARCUS THORNE, SENIOR APPROACH CONTROLLER
Date: October 12, 2023
Time: 10:15 AM
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Seattle, Washington
Interviewer: Investigator J. Vance, NTSB Aviation Safety Board

Q: Please state your full name, current title, and your specific role on March 3, 2023.
A: Marcus Thorne. I’m a senior approach controller, been with the TRACON for about twelve years now. On the third, I was working the final approach sector for Runway 27L. So, basically, I was handling the handoff from center to tower. I had the scope, the comms, the whole package. It was a standard mid-shift rotation, except for the weather.

Q: Walk me through the sequence of events as you experienced them. Start from when you first acquired the aircraft on your radar.
A: Yeah, okay. Let me pull up my shift log real quick. It was around 14:08 local time when I first saw the target. Flight 819, a regional turboprop, coming in from the northeast on the standard arrival route. I had a Southwest Airlines flight, SWA 442, on my scope too, but they were on a different glide path, so no conflict. The weather was just... it was brutal. We had a freezing rain band moving through, heavy snow, low ceilings. The radar was painting everything in magenta and red. I remember looking at the precipitation returns and thinking, "This is going to be a long afternoon." The pilot checked in, sounded calm. Standard readback. But then, maybe ten minutes out, he keyed the mic again. Said they were picking up ice. Not just a little bit. He said, "We're getting severe airframe icing, request vectors for diversion." I cleared him immediately. Gave him a heading to the alternate, which was about forty miles south.

Q: What did you observe on your radar and communications after the diversion request?
A: Right. So, after I gave him the turn, his altitude started dropping. Not a controlled descent, really. It was... it was faster than I expected. I asked him to maintain two thousand, and he acknowledged, but the readback was strained. You could hear it. Heavy breathing, maybe a little background noise. The radio had a lot of static, too. I think the precipitation was messing with the VHF. I kept calling him, "Flight 819, say altitude." No response for maybe... thirty seconds? Then he came back, "We're losing control, we're going down." And then the radar target just... it started descending rapidly. I mean, it wasn't a spiral or anything I could really tell from the scope, but the ground track got erratic. The blip started drifting left, then right, like it was fighting the wind. Then it just vanished. I called it in to the supervisor, declared emergency, got the crash alarm going. It was... it was quiet after that. Just the hum of the equipment and the weather radar pinging.

Q: You mentioned the aircraft was a regional turboprop. Were you aware of the engine type or any performance limitations in those conditions?
A: I mean, I know it's a twin turboprop. I think it's got Rolls-Royce engines on it? Or maybe it's the AE series... wait, no, the AE is Rolls-Royce, yeah. I don't work the maintenance side, so I don't get into the nitty-gritty, but we get bulletins. I remember a few months prior, there was a memo about ice accumulation on the propellers and how it affects thrust and vibration. But honestly, in the moment, you're just watching the blip. You don't think about the manufacturer. You think about the altitude, the heading, the terrain. The terrain warning was... well, we don't get terrain alerts on our scope, but I knew the area. It's hilly. Short of the alternate, there's a ridge. I knew exactly where he was going to hit.

Q: After the incident, investigators reviewed the cockpit voice recorder. Did you have any interaction with that data?
A: Yeah, later on. I was brought in to listen to the CVR... the voice recorder, I mean. They played the last few minutes. It was... hard to listen to. You could hear the stall warning, the GPWS, the crew trying to troubleshoot. The captain was calling out airspeed, the first officer was trying to adjust the power. There was a lot of ice shedding sounds, like... like hail hitting the windshield. I recognized the controller's voice, my own, asking for altitude. It was surreal. Hearing it back, you realize how fast it all happened. Maybe two minutes from the "losing control" call to impact. The audio quality was rough, but you could tell they were working the checklist. They weren't panicking. They were just... out of options.

Q: During the investigation, there was discussion about certification standards, specifically 14 CFR 25.571. Were you familiar with that regulation?
A: Not really, no. I'm a controller, not an engineer. But the investigators explained it to me. It's about damage tolerance and fatigue, right? Or... wait, no, 25.571 is about structural integrity and icing conditions, I think. They were talking about how the airframe was certified for certain ice accretion rates, and whether the actual conditions exceeded that. I just nodded along. My job is to keep the sky organized, not to certify the metal. But it made sense. If the ice builds up faster than the design envelope, the wings just... they stop working. You can't control what you can't see. I remember asking them if the deicing boots were supposed to cycle automatically, and they said yes, but the ice was just too thick. It was like trying to scrape a windshield with a credit card in a blizzard.

Q: You mentioned the alternate airport. Where was it located, and what was the weather like there?
A: The alternate was down south, near the coast. Actually, the aircraft type was originally developed and tested out of Renton, Washington, I think? Or maybe that's where the training simulators are. Wait, no, Renton is Boeing country. This was a regional turboprop. I'm mixing things up. The alternate was just a smaller field, better weather, or so we thought. But the storm was moving fast. By the time they turned, the ceiling had dropped to maybe eight hundred feet, visibility a mile. They were trying to get below the clouds, but the icing was too heavy. I remember thinking, "They should've gone higher, not lower." But you don't second-guess in real time. You just clear them. You trust the crew.

Q: Is there anything else you'd like to add about the sequence of events or your observations?
A: Just... the timeline. It was 14:08 when they checked in. 14:16 when they reported severe icing. 14:19 when they lost control. Impact was around 14:21. I've replayed it in my head a hundred times. The radio calls, the radar returns, the silence. I've worked in this facility for over a decade, and you see a lot of things. But this one... it sticks. I hope the voice recorder data helps them figure out exactly what happened with the deicing systems. I know the crew did everything they could. You could hear it in their voices. They weren't panicking. They were working the problem. The problem just... it was bigger than them.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Thorne. We'll follow up if we need clarification.
A: Yeah, sure. I'll be here.

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
REGULATORY COMPLIANCE AND OVERSIGHT DIVISION
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20591

CORRESPONDENCE REFERENCE: FAA-2023-0892-0014
DOCKET NO.: FAA-2023-0892
DATE OF ISSUANCE: October 12, 2023
CLASSIFICATION: REGULATORY OVERSIGHT REPORT / SAFETY RECOMMENDATION RESPONSE

SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This document constitutes the Federal Aviation Administration’s formal response to National Transportation Safety Board Safety Recommendation A-23-045, issued in conjunction with the investigation of NTSB Accident Number ERA23FA142, dated March 3, 2023. The referenced regulatory framework encompasses 14 CFR Part 25.1419 (Ice Protection), 14 CFR Part 121.629 (Operation in Icing Conditions), and 14 CFR Part 121.344 (Airborne Weather Radar and Ice Detection Equipment). This correspondence addresses compliance verification, airworthiness directive implementation, and systemic regulatory oversight pertaining to airframe icing recognition, crew resource management, and diversionary decision-making protocols. The subject matter is cross-referenced with Docket No. FAA-2023-0711, which governs supplemental type certificate (STC) modifications for enhanced ice accretion monitoring systems across transport-category aircraft.

BACKGROUND
The regulatory architecture governing flight operations in known or forecast icing conditions is established under 14 CFR Part 25.1419, which mandates that type-certificated aircraft demonstrate adequate ice protection for all critical flight surfaces, propulsion systems, and sensing equipment. Historically, the certification baseline has relied upon Appendix C of Part 25 to define atmospheric icing envelopes, with subsequent amendments addressing supercooled large droplet (SLD) conditions following multiple loss-of-control events. Prior NTSB Safety Recommendations A-18-012 through A-18-015 prompted the issuance of Airworthiness Directive 2019-14-08, requiring operators to revise Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions and implement enhanced crew training for inadvertent ice encounters.

While the March 3, 2023, accident involved a regional turboprop configuration, the certification and operational oversight principles remain harmonized across transport-category platforms. Comparative analysis of ice detection and anti-ice system architectures, including those integrated into the Boeing 737 MAX 9, demonstrates that modern type certificate holders employ automated ice accretion monitoring, whereas legacy turboprop fleets frequently rely on pilot visual recognition and manual activation of pneumatic or electro-thermal deicing systems. Engine manufacturer certification standards, as promulgated by Rolls-Royce under 14 CFR 33.68, require rigorous validation of inlet anti-ice performance under continuous maximum icing conditions. These engineering benchmarks inform the FAA’s ongoing evaluation of propulsion system vulnerability during high-angle-of-attack approach phases.

Operational oversight of foreign and domestic carriers, including entities such as Ethiopian Airlines Group, is conducted under bilateral aviation safety agreements and 14 CFR Part 129.39, which mandate adherence to equivalent airworthiness and operational standards. The Group’s documented implementation of advanced weather radar integration and standardized icing recognition protocols has been utilized as a reference model during recent FAA oversight audits. Nevertheless, the regulatory framework continues to identify systemic vulnerabilities in real-time ice accretion quantification, particularly during terminal area operations where meteorological data latency and crew workload intersect.

FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
The investigation into the March 3, 2023, loss-of-control event reveals that the flight crew encountered severe airframe icing during a stabilized approach, resulting in asymmetric lift degradation and subsequent aerodynamic stall. The First Officer, serving as pilot monitoring, correctly identified rapid ice accretion on the wing leading edges and initiated a diversion request; however, execution was delayed due to inadequate crew coordination and ambiguous MMEL guidance regarding degraded ice protection system performance. Post-accident telemetry and cockpit voice recorder analysis indicate that the aircraft’s existing ice detection system failed to provide quantitative accretion rate data, relying instead on qualitative visual cues that proved insufficient under rapidly deteriorating meteorological conditions.

Compliance verification conducted under 14 CFR 121.344 and 14 CFR 121.417 confirms that the operator maintained valid airworthiness certificates and adhered to published maintenance intervals. However, regulatory oversight actions, including unannounced ramp inspections and operational audits, identified deficiencies in recurrent training curricula. Specifically, simulator scenarios did not adequately replicate high-workload icing encounters during approach phases, nor did they emphasize immediate diversionary authority when ice accretion exceeds certified protection limits. The operator’s MMEL permitted dispatch with certain ice detection components inoperative, a provision that, while technically compliant, introduced unacceptable operational risk during marginal weather operations.

A critical gap in the current regulatory framework pertains to the absence of mandatory real-time ice accretion monitoring for aircraft operating under 14 CFR Part 121 in known icing conditions. While modern jet transports, including the Boeing 737 MAX 9, incorporate automated ice detection and advisory systems as part of their original type certification, many regional turboprop fleets operate under legacy supplemental type certificates that lack equivalent technological integration. Furthermore, engine anti-ice protocols, as validated by manufacturers such as Rolls-Royce, are not uniformly synchronized with airframe deicing activation sequences, creating potential for asymmetric thrust degradation during critical flight phases.

The FAA’s oversight division has determined that existing 14 CFR 25.1419 certification standards, while robust for continuous maximum icing, do not adequately address transient SLD encounters or rapid ice accretion during approach and landing configurations. The regulatory lag in updating Appendix C testing requirements, combined with inconsistent operator training standards, constitutes a systemic vulnerability that contributed to the March 3, 2023, accident. The First Officer’s timely recognition of the hazard underscores the necessity of standardized, data-driven decision-making protocols that prioritize immediate diversion over continued approach in deteriorating conditions.

ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to 14 CFR 121.629 and 14 CFR 25.1419, the Federal Aviation Administration hereby mandates the following corrective actions and compliance timelines:

1. Airworthiness Directive Implementation: All affected operators shall comply with AD 2023-14-05 within ninety (90) calendar days of issuance. This directive requires the installation of FAA-approved quantitative ice accretion monitoring systems or the implementation of equivalent procedural mitigations for aircraft lacking automated detection capabilities. Operators must submit compliance documentation, including installation records and functional test reports, to the responsible Flight Standards District Office (FSDO).

2. Training Curriculum Revision: Under 14 CFR 121.409 and 14 CFR 121.417, operators shall revise recurrent training programs to include high-fidelity simulator scenarios depicting rapid ice accretion during approach and landing phases. Training modules must emphasize immediate diversion authority, crew resource management protocols for icing emergencies, and standardized callouts for ice detection system degradation. Completion of revised training shall be documented and submitted for FAA review within one hundred twenty (120) days.

3. MMEL and Operational Procedure Updates: Operators shall amend their Minimum Equipment List to prohibit dispatch with inoperative ice detection or airframe deicing components when operating into forecast or known icing conditions. Revised operational procedures must be integrated into company manuals and distributed to all flight and dispatch personnel within sixty (60) days. The FAA will conduct targeted ramp inspections to verify compliance.

4. Cross-Fleet Certification Review: The Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) shall initiate a comprehensive review of ice protection system architectures across transport-category aircraft, utilizing the Boeing 737 MAX 9 certification baseline and Rolls-Royce engine anti-ice validation data as reference standards. This review will inform proposed rulemaking to update 14 CFR 25.1419 testing requirements for SLD conditions and mandate standardized ice accretion monitoring for all newly type-certificated aircraft.

5. Follow-Up Inspection and Audit Schedule: The FAA will conduct quarterly operational audits of affected operators for a period of twenty-four (24) months. Audits will evaluate training compliance, MMEL adherence, and real-world icing encounter reporting. Findings will be compiled into a biannual regulatory oversight report submitted to the NTSB and the Office of Aviation Safety.

Compliance with these directives is mandatory. Failure to adhere to the prescribed timelines will result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR 13.19 and potential suspension of operating certificates. The Federal Aviation Administration remains committed to advancing airworthiness standards, enhancing crew decision-making protocols, and ensuring that regulatory frameworks evolve in alignment with operational realities.
